The Hinge of the Jaw

Elias stood before the heavy oak door, the iron padlock cold against his palm. From the darkness behind the wood, his grandmother’s voice drifted up, smelling of dried lavender.

Stay for tea, Elias, she murmured, the same lilt that had tucked him in for twenty years, despite her burial in the churchyard last spring.

He fumbled with the rusted key, needing to see her face one last time to soothe the ache in his chest. The bolt slid back with a heavy, final groan.

He swung the door wide to find the stone room perfectly, hauntingly empty, his flashlight cutting through nothing but settling dust and cold air.

Then, the voice spoke again, not from the shadows, but from the hinge of his own jaw. Stay for tea, he whispered, his own hands moving to lock himself inside.
